utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-96-21-A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances, please. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. I'm Upawansa Yapa, appearing for the Prosecution, with Mr. Christopher Staker, Mr. Norman Farrell; Mr. George Huber, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I'm John Ackerman, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And is your client here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He is not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. For Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Tom Kuzmanovic here on behalf of Mr. Mucic. Mr. Morrison is sitting as a judge and is not available today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to ask you to repeat that, but you didn't have your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am Salih Karabdic, barrister from Sarajevo. With me is my colleague, Tom Moran, from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And for Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Cynthia Sinatra, and along with Peter Murphy, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, each of the appellants who are present, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT MUCIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT DELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT LANDZO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. The principal purpose of this preliminary conference is to sort out, if we can, the order in which the various groups of the grounds of appeal will be argued, the identity of the counsel who are going to take the principal burden of the argument, and the estimates of time. We have got a motion which was filed by the three appellants who are present, but that was stood to one side whilst you all considered the matter. I notice, from an assignment for you, Mr. Ackerman, that you say you will not be here for the whole week, or you will not be available for the whole week that the appeal has been fixed. That sounds as if what I'd suggested on the previous occasion should be adopted, and we put the grounds of appeal relating to your client on first. There is what I might group as the command responsibility, Common Article 3, and protected persons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be here through noon Thursday of the week we're arguing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So we can put it on at the Court's convenience, as long as I can be finished with all the Delalic issues by noon on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I should hope that you will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I should hope so too. I know, however, there are going to be some evidentiary matters that may be somewhat lengthy, and I just wanted to make sure that I had concluded with the Delalic issues prior to that. Beyond that, I really don't -- it's not important to me the order in which we do things. But most of the Delalic issues are unique to that case in any event. There is a command responsibility issue in Delalic but it's just kind of at the periphery of that, and the main command responsibility issues, I think, are going to be argued primary by Mr. Moran. I will only spend a very brief time on the Prosecution's suggestion that the law is to be expanded in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. The matters in which evidence is likely to be called would be the Judge Odio-Benito grounds, both of them, and Judge Karibi-Whyte grounds. I think those are the only ones, so they obviously should go to the bottom of the list. The proposal I put forward last time, for everybody's consideration, was that we should start with the command responsibility. That's the Prosecution's burden, I would think, Mr. Yapa. Have you any problem going first on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: We do not have any problem because we have appealed against the acquittal of Delalic, and this is one of the grounds that we'll be urging. So we do not have any problem starting first, or going first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. We will have command responsibility first, the Prosecution leading off. Mr. Ackerman, you say you are going to say very little about this, but you are a respondent to the Prosecution appeal. Do you want to carry the burden on behalf of the appellants, or is there some agreement between you as to who else should be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my part of that would be quite brief because I'm only concerned about the Prosecution's allegation that there should be some expansion of that concept. Mr. Moran will basically carry the burden for the other defendants on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Tom Kuzmanovic. One of our grounds of appeal is on the command responsibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I'm definitely going to be arguing that. Mr. Moran and I have already discussed what various portions of that are going to be split between us, but either Mr. Morrison or I are going to be arguing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there any agreement as to the order in which you want to address? You will recall that I did say on the last occasion that we expect the first counsel to carry the burden of the argument; we don't want other counsel merely repeating that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- but they may, of course, add anything which relates to their own clients or matters which they feel should be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think Mr. Moran will be arguing the legal sufficiency arguments and I will be arguing the factual sufficiency arguments. That's basically the difference between the two of us, and Mr. Moran can talk about that in more detail if you like. But we're not going to be covering the same ground, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it may be helpful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think what I will probably be discussing generally will be the law, and we're simply asking for slight clarifications in the Trial Chamber's holding, where -- and I agree with the application of the law to the facts from the Trial Chamber, obviously. I don't think Mr. Kuzmanovic and I have very many disagreements as to the law that is to be applied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But is there any agreement as to who should go first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think it was agreed that I was to go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Moran. Well, then, Mr. Ackerman, you'll go third, of the appellants; is that satisfactory to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. The Prosecution, Mr. Moran, Mr. Kuzmanovic, and Mr. Ackerman. Then we head into different country with the Common Article 3 matters. This is, I think, your baby, Mr. Ackerman, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's part of the cross-appeal of Mr. Delalic, and I will argue that but I will argue it very briefly. I think I would not spend more than ten minutes on that issue. I think it's pretty thoroughly briefed and it's not something that is unfamiliar to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right. Certainly not. All right, then. Well, then, I think Mr. Mucic merely adopts Delic's ground, so there's not likely to be any additional material there, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No additional material, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And Mr. Delic has raised the same issues. How long do you think you'll be, Mr. Moran?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll just settle for whatever Mr. Ackerman says. Judge Ackerman, I'm sure, will cover it pretty well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And there is also this ground by Mr. Delic whether the Geneva Conventions apply where Bosnia was not a party to them at the relevant time. That should not take very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was thinking ten minutes, and I think it's pretty well briefed. Mainly just for questions from the Court as much as anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: From the Prosecution's point of view, how long do you think you'll be addressing on this one, Mr. Yapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I would put it at ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This one should finish well within the hour then.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I should have asked about the command responsibility. How long do you think that's going to take, from the Prosecution's point of view, Mr. Yapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: We have tried our best to be as concise as possible in our written submissions, so I should say if there are any matters to be clarified, about 30 minutes, 30 to 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. What about you, Mr. Moran? I realise that you will depend upon what the Prosecution says, but I'm just trying to sort out how many days we should list for each day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I expect I will not take much more time than the Prosecution. Again, I think it will mainly be questions from the Tribunal, from the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And from your point of view, Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, roughly the same time, possibly a little less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman will be very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A little shorter, 15, 20 minutes. Maybe 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. We better say two hours for that. That's the estimate. Now, also the roughly associated group, the protected persons matter. Well, I think you were first off the mark again, Mr. Ackerman, on that one, because Mr. Mucic has adopted your ground. Mr. Delic, I think, has almost copied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may take five to ten minutes on that, and I think Mr. Moran intends to argue that, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, you mean first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I will probably go first for five or ten minutes, but I think Mr. Moran is maybe going to argue more extensively than I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, how extensively?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I was thinking, Your Honour, on the treaty interpretation, I might have about 20 minutes, and then Mr. Karabdic will have 10 to 15 minutes explaining the actual law of citizenship as it applied to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Sinatra, this is your first ground, I think, the first matter that you're involved in, your Ground 6. How long do you think you'll be?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that -- Ground 6 is which one, Your Honour? I don't have the brief in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: "The Trial Chamber erred in law in finding that the victims of the alleged crimes were protected persons for the purposes of the Geneva Conventions."

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I will defer to Mr. Moran and Mr. Ackerman on that argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of this ground, the response will depend on the time and the substance of the argument that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's understood Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: So it may be half the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Half the time. Thank you. Let's say about an hour and a half at the outside. Then there's the international character of the conflict. I think that might be you, Mr. Moran. I think you seem to have the most to say about it in the written submissions. Will you be going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since Judge Ackerman will be gone, I will be going first, and I won't be going very long. It's not something that the Appeals Chamber has not dealt with before. I think the Appeals Chamber is pretty familiar with the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You all will have seen, I assume, the recent decision in Aleksovski which deals with the question of judicial precedent, so that you will have to deal with that one along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I understand that. In fact, we've thought about the issue of precedent at some great length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Sinatra, this is also one of yours, Ground 5: "The Trial Chamber erred in law and in fact by finding that an international armed conflict existed with reference to the events alleged to have occurred at the site of each camp."

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will have nothing further to add to Mr. Moran's argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether Mr. Mucic has added this or not. Ground 10 might have adopted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it did, Your Honour, and we will simply rely on Mr. Moran's argument on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The Prosecution will be similarly short, I think, Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That one is well within the hour. Now, we start on the evidentiary matters. The Judge Odio-Benito and the Vice-president of the Republic of Costa Rica. We've got the expert, whose already the subject of a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What's going to happen there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't know yet whether the Prosecution wishes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They've got until Monday to let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, they do. And if they do not require him, Your Honour, we will rely on his written report and will not call him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Prosecution has never identified any expert which they wish to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: At the moment, what I can say is we may file an opinion on Monday. We've not taken a final decision yet. We have time till Monday, so we'll decide on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. How long will the argument go on this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are some other witnesses also -- oh, is Your Honour just referring to Judge Odio-Benito at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I put it in this way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I assume you will be leading on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I will. I will be doing all the arguments on these ground dealing to both Judge Odio-Benito and Judge Karibi-Whyte. Your Honour, I had thought of these as a group in a sense that they are, in a way, separate from the substantive merits of the case, and I was proposing to address them really as a group, and I had estimated the time that I would need to deal with all three of those grounds of argument as about one hour. Your Honour, there will be, of course, other witnesses in regard to the ground involving Judge Karibi-Whyte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll come to that in a minute, but if I can take them a little more logically. There's the evidence that you wish to put forward about Judge Odio-Benito and the Relief of the Victims of Torture Fund.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been having some communications with Mr. Staker and Mr. Yapa, and we anticipate that very early next week we will be putting before the Court an agreement as to several evidentiary issues which ought to suffice for all purposes. I don't anticipate that any further evidence will be necessary on that ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, now, on the Judge Karibi-Whyte matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we get to that issue, Mr. Murphy and I have discussed this yesterday. Mr. Morrison will be talking to Mr. Murphy on the Judge Odio-Benito issue and will handle a portion of that oral argument. What portion that is we're not certain yet, but he will, obviously, not cover the same ground that Mr. Murphy covers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You don't know how long he's likely to be then, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I intercede for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're now going into the two matters that you indicated would be last on the list. There are a number of issues in the Delalic appeal that we haven't talked about dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right. I'm going in the order in which I had them grouped originally, but you're right. These will be the last two. Can I just finish dealing with them and then come back to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Murphy. The Judge Karibi-Whyte ones, you say that you are putting forward some oral evidence, apart from Mrs. Sinatra's evidence about waiver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, and we will file a list of those witnesses, together with their statements, on Monday as per the scheduling order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How long do you think that they will all take?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, including Mrs. Sinatra, I would hope to do all that evidence perhaps in half a day or at the worst a little more. It will depend, of course -- I'm trying make a reasonable allowance for cross-examination by the Prosecution, but it shouldn't really take any longer than that. Maybe no more than two or three hours, but Mrs. Sinatra will be, obviously, at some length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the argument, you say, will take about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. But that includes all three of those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Delic and Mr. Mucic have joined the bandwagon, if I may so describe it, by adding a ground. Will you be adding to the evidence or to the argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We'll stand on Professor Murphy's argument and evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And we will do likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: There are just two other matters, if I might, before we leave those grounds. One is a very short matter of protocol in which I would appreciate the Court's guidance. Would it be the Court's preference when she testifies, Mrs. Sinatra should wear a robe or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Certainly she should not. She comes as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought so, but I wanted to be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Once when I was sitting at the bar table and I was obliged to give evidence in the case, much to my embarrassment, I asked a similar question and I was told I should remove my wig, but that was a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But they didn't expect me to get undressed completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will make sure Mrs. Sinatra removes any wig she may be wearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Or get undressed completely either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second matter I wanted to raise, and I do this with great diffidence because I know Your Honour has put forward an order in which these things should be taken, Your Honour, I would like to submit that there would be some merit in taking this group of ground relating to the Judges first for this reason: Your Honour, they are separate from substantive merits of the case, and they effect, of course, all the accused. Your Honour, there is a possibility, and I put it no higher than that, that it may be that the Appeals Chamber would find that one or more of these grounds is sufficiently compelling to require the reversal these convictions. Now, if that should happen, Your Honour may find it advisable to not pronounce on any wider issues of law as to which a full judgement of this Appeals Chamber might be obiter, because it may well be, Your Honour, that those issues of law, some of which are obviously of great importance, would have to be considered by a future Trials Chamber and possibly by a future Appeals Chamber. Your Honour, I make that suggestion only with great diffidence in the hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm puzzled as to how it affects the hearing, because I think you misunderstand the dynamics of an Appellate Court. It is very unlikely that we will come to some agreement after hearing the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It would have to be a very strong matter to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I respectfully agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It might be quite absurd for us to go away and consider it and then come back several weeks later and say, "We've come to this conclusion. Now we will or will not go on with the other matters." I think with the date being fixed, we should hear them all. You're quite right. If that were the result of the case, it would save us a lot of time and effort not to have to pronounce upon matters which, as you say, would be simply obiter, but it's not going to affect the hearing, if I may put it as boldly as that. So I think from the problem that we have or, shall I say, Mr. Ackerman has, which is a reasonable one seeing that we forced the date on, we should get him away and, therefore, all the evidentiary matters should be at the end of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, now, there's another matter which at least two of the appellates -- I'm sorry, yes Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: On this aspect, there are a few submissions that we wish to make on the calling of witnesses on these two matters. Mr. Staker will make them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are aware that the parties have until Monday to indicate what witnesses they will be calling and to file their statements. I don't know if it may be possible for the other parties to give some kind of indication today how many witnesses there may be and how long it may be expected. That may assist to some extent, now that we're trying to plan the course of the hearing, to have some knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In the motion which was filed, they did nominate, as I recall, a court reporter, a trial counsel, and Mrs. Sinatra. But I'm more interested, frankly, to see what the statements say, which will give us a better indication of where we're going.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That was going to be my next suggestion, Your Honour. I don't know if one possibility that might be worthy of consideration is whether the witness testimony might be given in affidavit form, in which case the Prosecution would then be able to examine whether there may be points which it might be in a position not to contest and any oral testimony would then be confined to cross-examination on points of contention. The alternative suggestion would be simply to invite the other parties to file witness statements which are as comprehensive as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They've been required to by the scheduling order to do that. I certainly agree with you. It may be worthwhile taking them as the evidence in the case if there's no dispute about it, but they certainly -- they do have to file witness statements, so we'll see what's in them to see where we're going.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me, if it will help the Prosecution, indicate this: that our intentions remain basically the same as we'd indicated in our previous communications to the Court. The witness statements that will be filed on Monday are, in fact, in affidavit form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hope they're more relevant than the earlier ones, Mr. Murphy. I mean when this issue first arose, you may recall in a separate opinion I almost gave an advice on evidence, which seems to have been completely ignored.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Court will find that the witness statements will cover the issues that we hope to address. Of course, the issues are confined to a quite narrow compass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. But even in the motion, you see, the emotional reaction of one of the witnesses is put forward as a matter of some importance. I would have thought, with all due respect, that that is totally and absolutely irrelevant. What we are concerned with is what people saw and heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think Your Honour will see from the witness statements that that is what the witnesses deal with. Your Honour, they are based entirely on the personal observation of the witnesses as to what was happening in the courtroom, and, Your Honour, that's really the scope of the evidence. The only additional matter, of course, is the testimony of Mrs. Sinatra regarding the waiver issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be more detailed, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that conclude the one about the two Judges? The next one where there's at least a joint approach is cumulative charging. That is an expression which I think is probably erroneous, because there is an issue, a very live one, about cumulative charging. We're dealing here with a cumulative convicting, and that's with Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delic. Who is going to take the burden of that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to take the lead on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How long do you think you'll take, Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And what will Mr. Delic be -- what will you be adding, Mr. Moran?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I add anything, it would be probably under five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. And the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It will be between 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I should say that there must be a distinction between cumulative charging and cumulative convicting, and most of the law that we've got at the moment relates solely to cumulative charging. So it is a new issue in that sense. Then there are the remaining individual grounds. Mr. Mucic has a series about grounds 5 and 6, the admissibility of the OTP interviews; ground 8, the conduct of the Defence; and ground 12, unlawful confinement. How long is that going to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Morrison will be handling those sections, and I would assume that all combined it will not take more than 35 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Maybe 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. All the written submissions are very detailed, I'm grateful to see. Now, Mr. Delic has got a series of grounds of appeal relating to the legal and factual sufficiency of the evidence, and that is his issues 9 and 10, 11 and 12, 13 and 14, 15 and 16, and 17 and 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, those were -- I think those were pretty well briefed. I don't expect to take much time on that. We do, of course, have the same issue that Mr. Mucic raised as to illegal confinement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If that's to be discussed at all by us, I'll discuss it behind Mr. Morrison, and if I do it will be very, very short. I don't expect long argument on any of those issues, and it might be easier just to deal with them as a group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- and plan on either Mr. Karabdic or I spending about 15 to 20 minutes on them total, at a maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's a little difficult to know the way in which it's been drafted. And when you say whether the evidence was legally sufficient, is that an issue as to what is required by the law, or whether you start off by saying there's a case to answer and therefore should it be accepted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the tradition I come from -- and it's probably a term of art in the United States, and if I've used it or abused it, I apologise -- but in the United States, evidence is legally insufficient if no rational fact-finder could find all the elements of the offence beyond a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No prima facie case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No prima facie case. If no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But why are we concerned about no prima facie case when we've got all of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, again, in the tradition where I come from, you get a legal review on appeal of whether any rational fact-finder could find all the elements, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But I don't see the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if no rational fact-finder, taking all the evidence, viewed in the light most favourable to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Then you had no case to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then there was no case to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you set out to answer it, so why are we concerned with it on appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I think we're dealing with a different tradition, and I may have -- I may not have handled this as well as I should have and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you. I'm just trying to find out what it is we're going to have to determine and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If, at the end of the trial, the Trial Chamber gave a perverse decision, then you will succeed. If they didn't and there was evidence to support a conviction, then you will lose. It seems to me that we don't need to deal with them separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, the remedy that I'm used to is a different remedy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One remedy would be if it was just -- if the fact-finder was just so wrong, even if there was legally sufficient evidence, there was a case to answer, if the appeals court just said, "This is just wrong," we would get a new trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I come from a different tradition, I'm afraid, and ten years in the Court of Criminal Appeal taught me that you don't seek to determine issues you don't have to if there is an answer to another ground raised. But anyway, we'll worry about that when --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Basically the two different issues in the tradition I come from would be the remedy as opposed to the -- and also the analysis would be slightly different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you see, you may have a problem there with the Tadic judgement. You see, the Tadic judgement has stated a basis for upsetting the Trial Chamber's decision on fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As I see it, if it was not a decision which a reasonable Trial Chamber could reach, then there would be the same remedy: There would be an acquittal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not a new trial point, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And we would have no objection if the Court ordered an acquittal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. But you see, you would get a new trial, which is the only other remedy of that all, only if the Trial Chamber had erred in law and it was not a matter which could be cured on an appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that if there was a decision on an issue of fact for which there was no legal basis, because there was an insufficient leading of evidence, you would get an acquittal; and if there was a decision on an issue of fact which no reasonable Trial Chamber could reach, then you would get it upset on the issue of fact and again an acquittal. So it doesn't seem to me that we have any problem about different remedies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, we have no problem with different remedies. Again, it's the tradition I come from. There's a slightly different analysis that I've talked about, and we would be more than willing to consider them as the same points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it's not quite the same, I agree with you, but one seems to me to be unnecessary if we find for you on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. All right. We've got that sorted out. Now, Mr. Landzo's individual grounds. The first one of selective prosecution, which is raised by grounds 1, 7, and 8. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will be addressing the individual issues for Landzo, which are particular to him, which would be selective prosecution, the issues dealing with diminished mental responsibility, and the sentencing issues, which -- it was properly briefed, I believe, but in addition to that, the only thing I will add is taking into consideration the new decisions that have come down since the brief has been filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course. How long do you think you'll be on selective prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I think with all three of these issues I would be a maximum of 30 to 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You understand that we're going to argue all sentencing together --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- as a group. So how long on these two?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: On selective prosecution, 10 minutes; on diminished responsibility, 30 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You realise that there is a very real issue here as to whether this is a "defence" at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm taking it because it says so in the Rules of Procedure. That's for the Prosecution to argue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They also talk about a defence of alibi. That doesn't mean it's a defence, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I didn't see that in their response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, but it's in the same Rule. I have read the Prosecution submissions as saying that it is merely a matter in mitigation, which of course is what it is even in the two common law countries of which I'm aware, where the special defence is a defence. They are only matters in litigation. So I want you to be very clear because you haven't dealt with this anywhere in your submissions. Of course, the Rules can't provide a defence which the international law does not provide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I appreciate you bringing that point up to me at this point, and I will take a look at this under a new light. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not the time here to debate it, but I think you seem to have overlooked this problem. When you say in England, Australia, and elsewhere where this defence exists, if it succeeds, then a conviction for manslaughter is entered, and you brush that to one side by saying you're entitled to an acquittal, that overlooks the fact that this is only ever a matter in litigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I believe if it lowers it to another offence, then that's not just a punishment issue, that is an issue of what it is exactly that the defendant is convicted of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, there is a lot of law on this and a lot of research on it, which I suggest you might like to have a look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I shall between now and June 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Indeed, there is a Law Reform Commission report which had to deal with the issue as to whether it should be abolished altogether and left solely to sentence, and it's something which you have not dealt with in your submissions at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You're right. I believe the last time I looked at it was in relationship to the international permanent criminal court, where they did, I believe -- the rules that they have promulgated will allow it to be an affirmative defence. And so I was basing my submissions on the research that I did on the International Criminal Court from the Rome Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That may be so, but there's a lot more than just the Rome Statute. How long do you think you'll be, then, on sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Prosecution and Mr. Mucic taking opposing views as to his sentence, how long would the Prosecution take?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that ground, we shall be 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Twenty minutes. And from Mr. Mucic's point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will take probably about the same time. Mr. Morrison will be handling the sentencing issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Delic also has an appeal against sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be in the neighbourhood of about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just a few general matters. If there is an agreement with the Prosecution about some documents for the Judge Odio-Benito points, could you file those in advance so that we can read them before the hearing? It will save a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, we will. I anticipate, Your Honour, that we'll probably do that quite early next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Delic has never filed a notice of grounds of appeal. We do have an index which I think sets them out, an index to the brief. But there really should be a document which is called "Grounds of Appeal," and that is what defines what the appeal is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At the time of the judgement, I consulted with some other persons here and read the Rule, and the Rule -- although the practice had been to list in the notice of appeal what the grounds were, the Rule did not seem to require that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it's interpreted that way, I think, in every other case. You should have a list of your grounds of appeal so we know what the grounds of appeal are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And because we didn't know at the time what our grounds of appeal would be, we just filed a general notice of appeal. However, I will file --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I accept that that is perfectly all right; you have to put a notice of appeal on within time. But then there should be some document somewhere which identifies your grounds of appeal, and merely having them in an index to your brief doesn't help. Of course, you've added two sets as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I will file that, with the Court's permission, within a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope you'll follow the same numbering as the ones you give in the index, because we're all working on that index.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will take the index and move it into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while I'm on my feet, there's one other question I'd ask the Court: It's come to my attention that in the last couple of weeks, some decisions have been handed down from American courts which may bear on the ex post facto issue, the application of the Geneva Conventions. Specifically, there is a new decision from the Supreme Court of the United States, which I have not read yet, frankly, that does deal with the issue. It's been my practice in the past, as you get closer and briefing is closed, that either at the time of oral argument or slightly before, if there is some authority that has not been discussed, just to simply file a list of citations to authority that are not cited in any briefs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- would that be helpful to the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It certainly would. It might be helpful also if we can have access to it. If it's on the Internet, we can get it from there, I suppose, but if it's been in a reported form, we'd like a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As of now, I think it's just on Lexus, I know, and it probably has not yet been printed by the West Publishing Company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If it has before the trial, we would be very grateful to you if we could have a copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- which we'll then distribute to all the Judges. Now, Mr. Mucic has filed a grounds of appeal but has to file another document consolidating that with the two that have been added. So would you make sure, Mr. Kuzmanovic, that there is another document filed which adds those two?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, there's been some tut-tutting, I suppose, about the form of your documents, calling it a cross-appeal. From those who are interested in the niceties of things, you can't have an appeal against an acquittal. What you're really saying, as I understand it, is in what, in Sydney, we called a notice of contention. What you're saying is that if the Prosecution succeeds on its appeal, then you want to argue that the judgement was wrong in other respects. That's not strictly a cross-appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I struggled quite a bit with trying to figure out how to go about what I did, but my concern was this: If we came to the point in the appeal where the Appeals Chamber determined that it was necessary that there be a new trial for Zejnil Delalic, there were issues that had been, I thought at the time, very central to his trial that needed to be decided by the Appeals Chamber so that they could be definitive then when the new trial came along. So that's the reason I filed the cross-appeal. If there's not to be a new trial, then the issues in the cross-appeal are of no moment at all to Mr. Delic, we don't care about them. We only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can we agree that they should not be called a cross-appeal but perhaps some other form of title? My suggestion is a notice of contention. So that we have to determine them only if the Prosecution succeeds in its appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you may call them that if you wish, Your Honour. My intention is that they are of no moment unless the Appeals Chamber says, "We're going to order a new trial for Mr. Delalic, and in that new trial, the Trial Chamber will take note of our decision on these two issues."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Or it may be possible, I haven't looked at it closely enough, it may be possible for the Appeals Chamber to determine the matter if they do uphold the Prosecution appeal on the evidence which was at the trial. But it would also, at that same time, have to determine these issues which you've raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So we're agreed that that's the way we approach it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's certainly the intention I had at the beginning, and what it's called is really of no concern to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. We've got your note, Mr. Ackerman, about the parts of your brief that should be treated as confidential. I suppose if we just have a red stamp that says "Confidential" on those pages, that would be sufficient, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Does it include more than just the evidence that you attached to the brief? The references in the brief itself are confidential?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there are some extracts attached to the brief that are confidential. In the body of the brief, those are referred to and then footnoted to either the extracts or some other parts of the testimony of those persons, Witnesses D and DC-4, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you've nominated those pages where the content of the confidential -- or the closed session evidence, you've nominated those as being confidential as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, my position, Your Honour, as you probably know from listening to me before, is that too many things are confidential. But I was asked to tell you which pages that material appeared on, and I've now done so, and what the Court wants to do with that information is of no concern to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Yapa, the Prosecution's response may need some form of confidentiality as well. If you've dealt with the evidence in Mr. Ackerman's brief that was heard in closed session, then the pages upon which you've referred to its contents would have to be declared somehow confidential. Would it be possible, over the next week or so, for somebody to have a look through to see whether there are any pages which should be marked confidential?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's very important when you're writing a judgement that you have some notification of what is confidential and what is not, because it's very easy to include something which you shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The only other matter I want to raise are the sitting times. The proposal is that we sit from 10.00 until 11.30, then from noon until 1.00, from 2.30 until 4.00, and then from 4.30 to 5.30. That gives us five hours a day. But on Wednesday, assuming we're still going on Wednesday, that last session, the 4.30 to 5.30 one, will not be possible because one of the Judges has another matter, which unfortunately cannot be moved, at that time in another courtroom. Are there any other matters, this being a Status Conference, that anybody wants to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of issues in the Delalic appeal that we haven't talked about yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, dear, yes. I thought we'd covered everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecution appealed and has contended that the Trial Chamber erred when it prevented the Prosecution from presenting rebuttal testimony or reopening its case. They've complained that Delalic should not have been acquitted as to Count 48 and that the Trial Chamber's definition of "knew or had reason to know" was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all command responsibility, at least the last part of it is. I don't know what Count 48 is from memory. Unlawful confinement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. You want those dealt with at the time, perhaps with or straight after command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you identify the grounds of appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's the Prosecution's brief, Your Honour. I think the way I have identified them in my reply is number 4, whether Delalic -- no. Number 5, the Trial Chamber correctly prevented the Prosecution from presenting rebuttal testimony or reopening its case. Number 6, the acquittal of Delalic as to Count 48. That tends to deal with protected persons, but it also deals with the question of aiding and abetting, and that's an important issue that needs to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that's -- apart from the definition of command responsibility, that means grounds of appeal 5 and 6 should be argued immediately after command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would think so. I'm not sure they are 5 and 6 in the Prosecutor's brief, but they deal with those issues, the reopen/rebuttal issue, the aiding and abetting issue, and this "knew or had reason to know," which I think probably I can include within the command responsibility remarks that I'll make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Within our own organisation, the way we've got command responsibility are the Prosecution grounds of appeal 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6, which I think includes all of those matters. So those are the ones which we propose to have argued at the beginning. Perhaps our general heading was a little off the mark. Now, is there anything that anybody else wishes to raise at this stage? Yes, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this relates to the matter that's just been discussed. It was our understanding that those grounds of appeal which you identified would be dealt with under the heading of command responsibility, although I did want to point out some of the Prosecution arguments in relation to those grounds of appeal. In fact, we rely on Article 7(1) of the Statute rather than 7(3).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes. That's actually noted on my sheet here. We've been trying to have the research that we've got arising out of the briefs under the various headings, and they are all in that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The other matter I also just wanted to mention is in the Prosecution response brief, I think. In particular, there are a number of general preliminary headings dealing with matters such as judicial notice and standards of review on appeal. Our understanding would be that it's not necessary to address these specifically in oral argument. To the extent that the issues come up under grounds of appeal, they can be referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I've heard Mr. Yapa on them before. If I may say so to all the parties, the written submissions have been very helpful. And don't worry, they are being read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There is another matter that Mr. Yapa would like to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's indulgence to mention one matter, a general matter. There has been a query about the composition of the Prosecution team. I have mentioned the names of three persons, including myself, as appearing for the Prosecution. Earlier there was Mr. Rod Dixon as a member of the appeals team for the Prosecution. He is no longer in the service of the Prosecution. But there is one other gentleman who is in the appeals team, but he served as a court deputy for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I saw him name there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Roeland Bos. And he was in the Celebici case for a very short period, but I have not mentioned -- marked his appearance here, but he's in the Appeals Chamber. Of course, subject to any objection from my learned friends in the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: At what stage of the trial was he the court deputy?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I could mention the dates. He was there from the 10th of March, 1997 to September 1997, in all 29 court days he has been in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, counsel for the Defence should consider that matter. It's something worth considering, although I should say that my experience with this Tribunal is that the Court Deputy plays no part in the resolution of the case. They are very important people to have, and they certainly know the evidence probably better than anybody, certainly the documents, but they do not play any part at all in the writing of the judgement. But if there's anything that you want to raise, I suggest you contact Mr. Yapa well and truly before hearing the appeal so that the issue can be resolved one way or the other. Whilst you're on this, having names on documents, Mr. Yapa, not so much in this case but we do have a problem when do you not put the names of counsel on the documents and yet you expect us to put them on the decisions, because we don't know who to include.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It seems to have been only a fairly recent development in the OTP that they don't put all the names on the documents. May I suggest that somebody reconsider so that we know what names to put on the decisions and judgements?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. Of course, this matter has been resolved. The question came up earlier as to what names should be put onto the decision when the decision is made, and there is no problem as such, but the decision to put down only one name when papers are filed is a decision that has been taken in the Prosecution, but this matter will be reconsidered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We would be very grateful. Either that, or you give us some document with the names of counsel that you want on the decision. Otherwise, we are either going to offend someone by deleting them or offend them putting them on when they had nothing to do with it, especially if they've lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any other matters to be raised? I'm very grateful to you all. We'll count that as -- the time will start to run on -- What is it? -- Rule 65 bis, Status Conferences, again from today, and we shall see you on the 5th of June. I'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: adjourned at 11 a.m.
